headline: Nasty night on Wall Street drags the ASX down — but GTA VI just broke every entertainment record in history, giving your Take-Two holding a boost.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: Biggest faller in today's session. AI-focused tech stocks took a beating as Wall Street sentiment turned cautious — reports from Business Insider note that some forecasters are starting to question how much longer the AI trade can run. The broader NASDAQ fell over 5% last night, dragging AI-heavy ETFs down with it.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: A rare bright spot today, up 2.3% at close. No single headline catalyst, but lithium stocks have been getting a little love as supply chain chatter around Pilbara's upstream position circulates. Still deeply underwater overall — down 61% on your total investment — but today's move is at least in the right direction.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Fell sharply today, tracking last night's brutal NASDAQ and S&P selloff. VTS mirrors the entire US sharemarket, so when Wall Street drops 3-5%, this ETF follows. The long-term story for US equities hasn't changed — this is the market digesting broader macro concerns.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped $13.78 last night in a broad tech selloff. No specific bad news for Microsoft itself — this was a market-wide move. Worth noting that NVIDIA has also crashed 48% recently and now trades cheaper than Microsoft on earnings multiples, which some analysts see as a sign the AI hardware premium is unwinding.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google fell $7 last night, part of the same tech-wide selloff. One analyst flagged that Alphabet's $9.1 billion cash burn is a concern compared to peers, though Google remains a cash-generating giant. The long-term AI and search advertising thesis is intact — this looks like market noise.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Fell 2.4% today as risk-off sentiment hit emerging markets. Rising geopolitical tension (Iran missile activity, Middle East conflict escalation) tends to push investors away from riskier emerging market assets. No change to the long-term diversification case.

movers.name: DHHF (Diversified High Growth ETF)
movers.note: Down 2.3% today, reflecting the global equity selloff filtering through its US and international holdings. DHHF holds a broad mix of global shares, so a rough night on Wall Street shows up here. Nothing structural — just the market having a bad day.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Slipped 2.1% today in line with the global market downturn. Similar story to DHHF — this is a diversified fund that moves with global markets. The underlying mix of growth assets is exactly what it should be for a long-term investor.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: The only US holding in the green last night, up 0.65%. GTA VI launched and absolutely smashed records — $3.8–5.7 billion in day-one sales (reports vary, but all agree it's the biggest entertainment launch in history). That's a massive tailwind for Take-Two, which owns the GTA franchise.

watch_today.title: GTA VI launch: biggest entertainment event ever — good news for Take-Two
watch_today.detail: GTA VI has pulled in somewhere between $3.8 billion and $5.7 billion on its first day, depending on the source — but every report agrees it's the single biggest entertainment launch in history, dwarfing any movie or album. Take-Two owns the GTA franchise, so this is a direct revenue event for your TTWO holding. The stock was up 0.65% last night despite the broader market falling 3-5%. Long-term, this validates the TTWO thesis completely.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX down 4% — worst day-mover in your portfolio
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF fell 4.1% today, and is now down 21.6% on your total investment. Some Wall Street forecasters are openly questioning whether the AI trade is running out of steam, and last night's NASDAQ crash of 5.3% hit AI-heavy stocks hardest. For a long-term holder, the AI theme is still very real — but this ETF is volatile and could stay under pressure if the tech selloff continues this week.

watch_today.title: Wall Street had a rough night — NASDAQ fell 5.3%, S&P fell 3.7%
watch_today.detail: Last night was one of the sharper single-session drops in recent memory. The NASDAQ fell 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7%, dragging almost everything — tech, growth, emerging markets, gold — down with it. The ASX followed suit today, closing down 1.6%. There's no single obvious trigger from the news data, but Iran missile activity and macro uncertainty are in the mix. As a long-term buy-and-hold investor, days like this are uncomfortable but normal — staying the course is almost always the right call.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX up 2.3% today — a small win in a rough session
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals bucked the trend today with a 2.3% gain. It's still down 61% on your total investment, which is a painful position. No major catalyst, just some positive supply chain commentary circulating. The lithium market is still broadly depressed — don't read too much into one good day, but it's good to see.

watch_today.title: RBA rate debate heating up — inflation data due soon
watch_today.detail: The RBA has now raised rates five times and there are signs the economy is feeling it — unemployment is ticking up and there are 'really bad signs' ahead of the next inflation data release. A divided RBA board means more uncertainty on the rate path. This matters to your ASX holdings and mortgage holders alike. Watch the inflation print when it drops — it could move the market.

watch_today.title: MSFT and GOOG: down on the night, long-term case unchanged
watch_today.detail: Both Microsoft (down 2.77%) and Alphabet (down 2.59%) fell last night as part of the broad tech selloff — not because of anything specific to either company. Microsoft is still a dominant AI and cloud player; Google still owns search and YouTube. For a long-term holder these are just market fluctuations. Sit tight.

world.summary: The Middle East remains on edge as Iran's missile capabilities expand and Bahrain reports civilian infrastructure damage from an Iranian attack. Ukraine continues to target Crimea supply lines, while global tech outages are increasing in frequency and severity.

stories.title: Iran attacks Bahrain — civilian industrial facility damaged
stories.why_it_matters: Iran launched an attack that struck a civilian industrial facility in Bahrain, marking a significant escalation of Iranian military action beyond its immediate neighbours. This follows analysis showing Iran has been expanding its missile ambitions far beyond the Middle East in the wake of ongoing regional conflict. For everyday people, it signals that the Middle East conflict is spreading geographically, which raises global energy security concerns — oil infrastructure in the Gulf region is always at risk when tensions flare like this.

stories.title: Ukraine strikes Crimea supply line — major blow to Russia
stories.why_it_matters: According to European intelligence assessments, Ukraine has dealt a significant blow to Russia's supply lifeline into Crimea — the peninsula Russia seized back in 2014. Crimea is strategically vital to Russia's southern military operations, and cutting supply routes there puts real pressure on Russian forces. The war is now well into its fourth year and Ukraine continues to find ways to strike at Russian logistics, suggesting the conflict is far from over.

stories.title: Global technology outages are surging — and nobody has a clear answer why
stories.why_it_matters: Major technology outages are becoming more frequent and harder to explain globally, covering everything from banking systems to critical infrastructure. For everyday people, it means more disruption to services we rely on — payments, communications, transport — and raises real questions about how fragile our digital infrastructure has become. It's also a risk factor for tech-heavy investment portfolios, as prolonged outages can hurt company revenues and reputations.

stories.title: UN talks on AI in warfare end with no binding rules agreed
stories.why_it_matters: United Nations talks on regulating artificial intelligence in warfare have ended without any commitment to legally binding rules. Countries couldn't agree on how to govern autonomous weapons systems — machines that can make life-and-death decisions without a human in the loop. The failure means there's no international legal framework to stop AI weapons from proliferating, which is a genuinely serious long-term risk for global security.

stories.title: Israel political crisis deepens — Eisenkot ready to lead emergency government
stories.why_it_matters: Israel's political situation is becoming increasingly unstable, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot signalling he's prepared to lead an emergency government as prime minister — explicitly ruling out a rotation with Netanyahu. This points to a deepening political crisis alongside the ongoing military conflict. Political instability at the top of a nation at war adds uncertainty to an already volatile region, with implications for Middle East diplomacy and energy markets.

markets.summary: Last night on Wall Street was ugly — the NASDAQ crashed 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% in one of the sharper single-session selloffs in months. The ASX followed suit today, closing down 1.6% at 8,592. Gold also copped a 4.6% hit, while oil held steady. The Aussie dollar slipped slightly to US66.2 cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: ASX followed Wall Street lower, closing down 1.6% today.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Sharp fall last night — broad market selloff hit all sectors.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech took the brunt of it last night — down over 5% in a single session.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil barely moved despite Middle East tension escalating — up just 0.2%.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold dropped sharply — unusual in a risk-off day, suggesting some forced selling or profit-taking.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar slipped slightly — still holding above 66 US cents.

politics.summary: The RBA is under intense scrutiny as five rate hikes bite the economy — unemployment is rising, the housing market is wobbling, and the central bank's own board is reportedly divided on the path forward. Inflation data due soon could be the next flashpoint.

stories.title: RBA rate hikes causing real pain — and the board is divided
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has now raised rates five times and there are growing signs it may have gone too far. Unemployment is rising in a way that is raising 'serious questions' about whether the RBA's tightening cycle (raising rates to slow the economy and cool inflation) is now actively hurting ordinary Australians. The RBA board itself is reportedly divided on what to do next — which means more uncertainty for anyone with a mortgage or a business loan. The next inflation data print will be critical in deciding whether rates stay put or move again.

stories.title: Inflation data coming — and there are 'really bad signs' already
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's upcoming inflation data release is being watched closely, and AAP is reporting there are 'really bad signs' ahead of it. If inflation remains stubbornly high, it gives the RBA cover to keep rates elevated or even hike again — bad news for mortgage holders, renters, and consumer-facing businesses. If inflation is falling faster than expected, it could bring forward rate cuts. Either way, this data point is a big deal for the Australian economy in the weeks ahead.

stories.title: Housing policies backfiring — buyers retreating, rental crisis worsening
stories.why_it_matters: Government housing policies are producing the opposite of what was intended — buyers are pulling back from the market while the rental crisis continues to deepen. Higher interest rates combined with uncertain policy settings are making it harder for first-home buyers to get in, and tighter conditions for investors are reducing rental stock. For anyone renting or hoping to buy, the near-term outlook is tough.

stories.title: Western Australia staring down a $1 billion stamp duty shortfall
stories.why_it_matters: WA Treasurer Saffioti's budget is reportedly facing a $1 billion hole from stamp duty collections falling well short of projections. When property transactions slow — because buyers are retreating — stamp duty revenue (the tax paid when you buy a property) collapses. This kind of shortfall forces budget cuts or new revenue measures, and signals just how much the property slowdown is hitting state government finances.

ai.summary: Big week in AI: Google launched Gemini 4 Neon to compete head-on with the latest Claude and GPT models, Anthropic hit the public markets, and global debate is heating up about how (or whether) to regulate AI — especially in warfare. Meanwhile, some on Wall Street are starting to question how much longer the AI investment boom can run.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon — takes on Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2
stories.why_it_matters: Google has released Gemini 4 Neon, its latest flagship AI model, directly competing with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol. This is the AI equivalent of a smartphone launch war — the big tech players are racing to have the most capable model. For users, it means better AI assistants, more capable coding tools, and smarter search. For Google as a business (and your GOOG holding), staying competitive in the AI model race is essential to its long-term relevance.

stories.title: Anthropic goes public — Wall Street starts asking if the AI trade is overcooked
stories.why_it_matters: Claude-maker Anthropic has debuted on public markets, becoming a major new listed AI company. Amazon's price target for its own stock was lifted to $310 by Oppenheimer partly off the back of Anthropic's IPO (Amazon is a big Anthropic investor). But at the same time, some Wall Street forecasters are openly starting to wonder if the AI investment boom is on its last legs — warning that sky-high valuations may not be sustainable. This directly affects your GXAI.AX holding, which is an ETF full of AI-exposed stocks.

stories.title: UN AI warfare talks collapse — no binding rules agreed
stories.why_it_matters: United Nations talks on how to handle AI in warfare ended without any binding agreement. Countries couldn't agree on rules around autonomous weapons — drones, targeting systems, or AI that can make military decisions without a human. The lack of any framework means the development of lethal AI systems is effectively ungoverned internationally, which is alarming to many security experts and campaigners who warn of an AI arms race.

stories.title: London protesters demand stricter AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Protesters took to the streets in London calling for stricter regulation of AI, citing growing safety concerns about how rapidly the technology is being deployed without adequate oversight. This is becoming a mainstream political issue — not just a tech debate — as more people worry about AI's impact on jobs, privacy, and safety. Regulation is coming eventually; the question is how strict and how fast, which matters for AI-exposed investments.

stories.title: India's Chief Justice: regulate AI, don't ban it
stories.why_it_matters: India's Chief Justice has weighed in on the global AI debate, arguing that regulation — not an outright ban — is the right approach to managing AI's risks. India is one of the world's biggest technology markets and a growing AI hub, so its legal and policy positions carry weight. The view aligns with what most Western governments are moving toward: guardrails rather than prohibition, which is generally seen as a positive for the AI industry's long-term growth.

sport.summary: NRL Grand Final confirmed: the Roosters beat the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. The 2026 AFL Draft wrapped up with plenty of talking points, and 14-year-old Leihani Zoric has made history as the youngest women's world surfing champion ever.

stories.title: ROOSTERS WIN THE 2026 NRL GRAND FINAL — 19-18 over the Knights
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have taken out the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in an absolute nail-biter at Accor Stadium. One point in it at the final whistle — it doesn't get much tighter than that. The Roosters claim another premiership in a dramatic finish that will be talked about for years.

stories.title: 14-year-old Leihani Zoric becomes women's world surfing champion
stories.why_it_matters: Australian surfing has another history-maker. Leihani Zoric, just 14 years old, has become the women's world surfing champion — the youngest in history. This is an extraordinary achievement from someone who isn't even old enough to drive. Surfing fans on the Gold Coast will be particularly proud of this one, given the region's deep connection to the sport.

stories.title: NRL players say season is too long — NRLW players say theirs is too short
stories.why_it_matters: A new player poll reveals an interesting split inside rugby league: NRL men's players feel the season is dragging on too long, while NRLW (women's) players want more games and a longer competition. It reflects the growing stature of the women's game — players want more of it — while the men's game faces a push to trim the fixture list to reduce player workload and injury risk. Expect this to fuel debate over the competition structure for 2027.

stories.title: 2026 AFL Draft done and dusted — three clubs get perfect grades, one major blunder
stories.why_it_matters: The 2026 AFL Draft is complete, and the reviews are in. Fox Sports has handed three clubs perfect draft grades for their selections, while flagging at least one major blunder that could come back to haunt a club. The draft is where AFL clubs build their future, so getting it right matters enormously for the next five to ten years of competition.

stories.title: NRL reveals ambitious 'global round' concept — three cities, three nights
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL has revealed plans for a 'global round' format — three matches across three different cities over three nights, taking rugby league overseas in a big way. The concept is aimed at growing the game internationally and mirrors what the AFL has done with games in the US and UK. Details on which cities are involved haven't been fully confirmed, but it's a bold step for the code's global ambitions.
